analogy.p: Imagine a bath filling while the plug is in. Mitigation is turning the tap down so less water pours in (fewer emissions), and carbon sinks are like a bit of the water draining away. Adaptation is putting towels and a barrier round the bath so the floor stays dry if it overflows. You really need to do both, because turning the tap down will not instantly remove the water already in the bath. The analogy breaks down because the atmosphere is shared by everyone, so one person turning down their own tap is not enough without everybody doing it.

bullets: Know the definition of **mitigation** (reduce the causes) and **adaptation** (cope with the effects) and never mix them up.
Know the four mitigation strategies: alternative energy, carbon capture, planting trees, international agreements.
Know the three adaptation strategies: farming changes, water supply management, protection from rising sea level.
Be able to **explain how** each strategy works, not just name it.
Be able to give **advantages and disadvantages** (cost, effectiveness, speed, who benefits) so you can evaluate.
Be able to link back to the causes: burning fossil fuels, deforestation and farming add CO2 and methane, so mitigation targets those sources.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA Geography 8035 asks you to know how climate change can be **managed**. There are two broad strategies. **Mitigation** means managing the **causes** of climate change, by reducing the amount of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. The specification lists four mitigation methods: **alternative energy production**, **carbon capture**, **planting trees** and **international agreements**. **Adaptation** means managing the **effects** (responses) of climate change by getting used to a changing climate. The specification lists three adaptation methods: **change in agricultural systems**, **managing water supply** and **reducing risk from rising sea levels**. It matters because it is the "so what" of the previous topic and a favourite 4 and 6 mark question.

bullets: **Mitigation** = reducing the **causes**: fewer greenhouse gases going up, or more removed (sinks).
**Adaptation** = responding to the **effects**: living with higher temperatures, changed rainfall and higher sea levels.
Mitigation benefits the **whole world** in the long term; adaptation protects a **specific place** sooner.
Mitigation is a **long-term** solution and results take decades; adaptation can have **quicker** local effects.
Wealthy countries can afford more of both; poorer countries often have to prioritise **adaptation** because they are hit hard but cause few emissions.
Exam trick: if the strategy involves **energy, CO2, trees or treaties** it is mitigation; if it involves **crops, water or flood defences** it is adaptation.
core.h: Mitigation versus adaptation: the key difference
core.p: The easiest way to separate the two is to ask "is this reducing the problem or coping with it?". Mitigation tries to **stop the problem getting worse** by cutting emissions of greenhouse gases or removing carbon dioxide from the air. Adaptation accepts that some climate change is already **locked in** (because CO2 stays in the atmosphere for a very long time and the oceans warm slowly) and prepares people and places for it. Neither is enough alone, so governments usually do both. Mitigation is a **global** job (CO2 mixes through the whole atmosphere, so one country cannot fix it alone), whereas adaptation is often **local or national** and protects the people paying for it.

bullets: **Wind power**: turbines turn kinetic energy of the wind into electricity. No CO2 while operating, free fuel, but **intermittent** (no wind, no power), can spoil views, make noise and harm birds and bats; offshore farms cost more.

**Solar power**: photovoltaic (PV) panels convert sunlight into electricity. Clean and panels can be put on roofs, but output depends on **sunshine**, no output at night, and the up-front cost is high.
**Hydro-electric power (HEP)**: falling water spins turbines. Reliable and can store water, but dams flood valleys, **displace people**, damage habitats and are expensive.

**Nuclear power**: splitting atoms makes heat for electricity. Very low CO2 in operation and reliable, but creates **radioactive waste**, is very costly to build and decommission, and accidents are rare but serious.
**Biofuels**: fuels from plants (bioethanol, biodiesel). In theory **carbon neutral** because the plants absorbed CO2 as they grew, but crops can use land that could grow food or cause deforestation.
**Geothermal, tidal and wave**: use heat from underground or movement of water; reliable in the right place but only suited to **certain locations**.
Common problem for all: **cost of setting up**, and the need for new grids and electricity storage (batteries) when supply is intermittent.
Cause and effect to quote: **alternative energy replaces fossil fuel burning, so less CO2 is emitted, so less heat is trapped**.
core.p: Most CO2 comes from burning **fossil fuels** (coal, oil and natural gas) for electricity, heating and transport. **Alternative energy** (also called low-carbon, renewable or clean energy) produces electricity with little or no CO2 released while generating. Switching from fossil fuels to alternatives therefore **reduces the amount of carbon dioxide added to the atmosphere**, which weakens the enhanced greenhouse effect. Alternatives include wind, solar, hydro-electric power (HEP), nuclear, biofuels, geothermal and tidal or wave power. The trade-off is that each has cost, reliability or environmental drawbacks, so countries usually use a **mix**.

bullets: Three stages to remember: **capture**, **transport**, **storage**.
CO2 is turned into a dense fluid by **compression** so a large amount can be stored in a small volume of rock.
Stored in **porous rock** (spaces to hold CO2) beneath **impermeable cap rock** (stops escape).
**Advantage**: can remove most of the CO2 from emissions and works with existing power stations and factories.
**Disadvantage**: **expensive**, uses extra energy to capture and compress CO2, and few large projects exist so far.
**Disadvantage**: risk of **leakage** over time and need for long-term monitoring; suitable storage sites are not available everywhere.
It does not reduce fossil fuel use, so it can **delay** the switch to renewables, and the CO2 from mining and transporting the fuel is not captured.
Do not confuse it with **planting trees**: CCS is a technological fix, trees are a natural carbon sink.
core.p: **Carbon capture and storage** is a technology that stops CO2 from reaching the atmosphere. CO2 is **captured** from the waste gases of power stations and heavy industry (such as cement and steel), **compressed**, **transported** by pipeline or ship, and **injected deep underground** into suitable rock where it is stored. Good storage sites are depleted oil and gas fields and deep **saline aquifers** (porous rock filled with salty water) that are sealed by a layer of **impermeable cap rock** so the gas cannot leak. CCS matters because fossil fuels and industry will not disappear overnight, so it lets them run with far fewer emissions.

bullets: Word equation: carbon dioxide + water (using light energy) gives glucose + oxygen; the **carbon** in the glucose is used to build the tree.
A **carbon sink** is anything that absorbs more carbon than it releases, for example growing forests and oceans.
**Advantages**: cheap compared with technology, many **extra benefits** (biodiversity, soil protection, flood reduction, recreation), can involve local communities.
**Disadvantages**: needs a lot of **land** that could grow food or house people; slow; carbon is released again if trees burn, die or are cut down and burned.
**Monoculture plantations** (one species) store carbon but support little wildlife and are more vulnerable to disease and fire.
Protecting existing rainforest from logging and clearing is often more effective than planting new trees because mature forests already hold huge amounts of carbon.
Planting trees alone cannot offset all emissions because the amount of land needed would be enormous.
core.p: Trees take in carbon dioxide from the air during **photosynthesis** and store the carbon in their wood, leaves and roots, which makes forests **carbon sinks**. Planting new forests (afforestation) and protecting existing forests (stopping deforestation) therefore removes CO2 from the atmosphere and keeps it locked up. The more trees there are, and the faster they grow, the more carbon they store. Trees also provide other benefits such as habitats for wildlife, reduced soil erosion and flood risk, and shade, which is why governments and charities support tree planting. However, young trees store little carbon at first, and it takes **decades** before a new forest makes a big difference.

bullets: **Kyoto Protocol (agreed 1997, in force 2005)**: legally binding targets for developed countries to cut emissions (about 5 per cent below 1990 levels on average); the **USA did not ratify** it and developing countries such as China and India had no targets.

**Paris Agreement (2015)**: aim to keep global temperature rise **well below 2 degrees Celsius** above pre-industrial levels and to pursue **1.5 degrees Celsius**; each country sets its own **nationally determined contribution** and reports and updates it regularly (every five years).
Paris includes almost all countries, including big emitters, and some **finance** to help poorer countries cut emissions and adapt.
**Strengths**: raise awareness, share responsibility, push governments to act and encourage investment in clean technology.
**Weaknesses**: targets can be **voluntary**, hard to enforce, countries may leave or not meet their pledges, and pledges so far are not enough on their own to meet the aim.
**National laws** also help, for example the UK Climate Change Act (2008) which sets legally binding carbon budgets and a target of **net zero by 2050**.
Net zero means any greenhouse gases still emitted are balanced by an equal amount removed (for example trees or CCS).
Disagreement: developed countries caused most historical emissions, while fast-growing economies now emit a lot, so who should cut most is a major argument.
core.p: Climate change is a **global problem**, because greenhouse gases mix throughout the atmosphere and no country can solve it alone. **International agreements** are treaties where countries agree to set targets to cut their emissions. Two you should know are the **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** and the **Paris Agreement (2015)**. Kyoto set **legally binding targets** for developed countries only, while Paris asks almost every country to set its own targets. Agreements are important because they make countries share the effort and give a common aim. Their weakness is that they depend on countries being willing to follow through, and richer and poorer countries often disagree over who should do more.

bullets: **New crop varieties**: drought-resistant, heat-tolerant or salt-tolerant crops (some produced by selective breeding or genetic modification) keep yields up in hotter, drier conditions.
**Changing crops**: growing crops suited to the new climate, for example a crop that needs less water.
**Changing timing**: planting earlier or later to avoid heat or use the rain, and using crop rotation to protect the soil.
**Efficient irrigation**: **drip irrigation** delivers water straight to roots so less is lost to evaporation.
**Soil and water conservation**: terraces, mulch and planting trees among crops (agroforestry) reduce erosion and keep moisture.
**Changing livestock**: breeds that cope better with heat and less grazing.
**Advantages**: protects food supply, farm incomes and local jobs; **disadvantages**: cost, need for knowledge and training, and some changes (such as more irrigation) put pressure on water supplies.
Link: this is adaptation because it does not stop climate change, it helps farming cope with the **effects**.
core.p: Climate change alters temperature and rainfall, which can reduce yields or make some areas too hot or dry for the current crops. **Adaptation in farming** means changing what and how food is grown so that production can continue and food supply is protected. Farmers can grow **drought-resistant** or **heat-tolerant** crop varieties, switch to different crops, change planting and harvest dates, and use **irrigation** more efficiently. Some places gain, for example growing seasons lengthening in cooler countries, so new crops can be grown there. The main limit is that poorer farmers often cannot afford new seeds, equipment or training.

bullets: **Reservoirs** store water in wet periods for use in dry periods; they are costly and flood land, and water evaporates from them.
**Desalination** removes salt from sea water; it gives a reliable supply near coasts but uses a lot of **energy** (and so may increase emissions) and produces salty waste (brine).
**Rainwater harvesting** and **grey water recycling** capture or reuse water at home or farm scale; cheap and simple but small volumes.
**Water transfers** by pipeline or canal move water from wet to dry areas; expensive and can harm the source area.
**Reducing demand**: **water meters** (people pay for what they use), **fixing leaks** (a lot of treated water is lost from old pipes), low-flow showers and toilets, hosepipe bans.
**Farming efficiency**: drip irrigation and growing less thirsty crops cut the largest user of water.
Evaluation: demand reduction is usually **cheaper and quicker**, supply schemes are **expensive and have environmental costs**.
core.p: Climate change is expected to make rainfall less reliable and increase evaporation in many regions, while population growth increases demand, so some places face **water stress**. Managing water supply means both **increasing supply** and **reducing demand**. Supply can be increased by building reservoirs, desalination plants and rainwater harvesting systems, and by transferring water between regions. Demand can be reduced by metering, repairing leaks and promoting water-saving appliances. Using both is more effective than either alone because supply options are expensive and use energy.

bullets: **Sea walls and embankments**: strong barriers that stop waves and surges; effective but expensive to build and maintain and can cause erosion elsewhere.
**Tidal and flood barriers** (for example the Thames Barrier in London) close to block storm surges.
**Raised buildings**: homes built on stilts or raised platforms and flood-proofed ground floors (a common approach in low-lying parts of Bangladesh).
**Mangroves and salt marshes**: natural vegetation absorbs wave energy, traps sediment and gives habitats; cheaper and sustainable but need space.
**Managed retreat**: allowing the sea to flood land and moving people and buildings inland; cheaper long term but people lose homes and farmland, so compensation is needed.
**Warning and planning**: flood forecasts, evacuation routes and shelters, and stopping new building on flood plains.
Poorer countries often use cheaper, community-based approaches such as raised homes and **cyclone shelters** instead of expensive barriers.
Link: the strategy protects against an **effect** (higher sea level), so it is adaptation.
core.h: Adaptation 3: reducing risk from rising sea levels
core.p: Sea level is rising because sea water **expands as it warms** (thermal expansion) and because **land ice melts** and adds water to the oceans. This increases the risk of coastal flooding, storm surges and erosion, particularly for low-lying coasts and deltas where millions live. Adaptation can use **hard engineering** (such as sea walls, tidal barriers and embankments), **soft engineering** (such as restoring salt marsh and mangroves, or beach nourishment), changes to buildings and planning, and **managed retreat**. Which method is chosen depends on the money available and the value of what is being protected.

bullets: **Cost**: nuclear, CCS and big sea defences are very expensive; tree planting, managed retreat and metering are cheaper.
**Speed**: demand-reduction, planting crops and local flood protection work quickly; trees and international agreements take decades.
**Scale**: global treaties tackle the whole problem, local schemes tackle one area.
**Fairness**: rich, high-emitting countries have the money and a historic responsibility; poor, low-emitting countries are often most vulnerable.
**Side effects** (unintended consequences): HEP floods valleys, biofuels compete with food, desalination uses energy.
**Uncertainty**: some methods such as CCS are not yet proven at large scale.
Use evaluative words: "however", "although", "the most effective", "in the long term", "depends on".
core.h: Evaluating strategies: cost, speed, scale and fairness
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to weigh up strategies, so use a small set of criteria every time. Think about **cost**, **speed**, **how big the effect is**, **who benefits**, and **side effects**. Mitigation is essential for the long term but its benefits are shared worldwide and appear slowly, so countries may be reluctant to pay for it. Adaptation gives clearer, local benefits but does not fix the cause, so the problem keeps growing. A good conclusion says that a **combination** is best and that the right balance depends on a country's wealth and its risk.

bullets: Rainforest link: protecting forests = mitigation (keeps carbon stored); adapting farming in the rainforest = adaptation.
Coasts link: sea walls and managed retreat are the same strategies used for coastal erosion and flooding.
Resources link: energy mix, water stress and food supply.
Global development link: richer countries have more resources to adapt, so the **impacts and responses are unequal**.
Sustainability link: a good strategy meets today's needs without harming the future, for example renewable energy and sustainable farming.
Use named examples if you know them (such as the UK net zero target, the Paris Agreement or the Thames Barrier) to add detail.
core.h: Links to other topics and real-world context
core.p: This point connects the physical and human parts of the course. It follows on from the **evidence and causes of climate change** and the enhanced greenhouse effect, because each mitigation method targets one cause: alternative energy targets fossil fuels, trees target deforestation, and agreements target all sources. It links to **tropical rainforests** (deforestation reduces a carbon sink and rainforest protection is a form of mitigation), to **hot deserts** (water supply and farming under stress), to **coastal management** (hard and soft engineering), and to **resource management** (energy and water). Case studies from your own work, such as a country's energy mix or a coastal protection scheme, can add place-specific detail and make your answers more convincing.

bullets: Structure: **point** (strategy), **how it works**, **evidence or example**, **evaluation** (strength or limit).
Always include a **conclusion** that answers the question: for example "adaptation is more realistic for a poor country, but mitigation is needed long term".
Use **specialist terms**: carbon sink, enhanced greenhouse effect, emissions, renewable, sustainable, mitigate, adapt.
Refer back to the **resource** (figure or text) in the question if one is given and quote data from it.
Do not just list: development and linking earn the top-level marks.
Spell "adaptation" and "mitigation" carefully, and don't use "mitigation" for responses to flooding.
core.h: Higher-level thinking: how to build a 6 mark answer
core.p: The 6 mark questions on this topic usually ask you to "assess" or "evaluate" a strategy, or to "explain" the difference between two. Marks are awarded for knowledge, for **applying** it to the situation in the question, and for a **judgement** supported by reasons. Plan in one minute: choose two or three strategies, give how each works, one advantage and one disadvantage, then finish with a clear conclusion. Aim to use linking words such as "because", "this means" and "therefore" so that each point is developed rather than just listed.

exam: Command words: **describe** = say what it is; **explain** = give a reason using "because" or "this means"; **assess/evaluate** = weigh strengths and weaknesses and reach a judgement.
1 mark: a correct term or fact (for example "carbon capture and storage"). 2 marks: a point plus development (what it does and why that helps).
4 marks: usually two developed points, each a method plus an explained effect, or a strength and a weakness.
6 marks: aim for balanced, developed paragraphs with named strategies, example detail and a final judgement; marked in levels, with the top level needing a clear and supported conclusion.
Model phrase: "Alternative energy such as solar replaces fossil fuel burning, so less carbon dioxide is released, which reduces the enhanced greenhouse effect."
Model phrase for adaptation: "Drought-resistant crops can still grow when rainfall falls, so farmers keep their yields and food supply is protected."
Always include a **limitation** for each strategy (cost, time, land use, energy use or side effects).
In "how far do you agree" questions, show **both sides** then decide; use "however", "but" and "overall".
Use percentage-change skills: change divided by original, multiplied by 100. Show your working.
Use the resource: quote numbers and trends from graphs and text, and refer to units (ppm, million tonnes).
Name a place or example where you can (UK net zero target, Thames Barrier, Bangladesh cyclone shelters).

mistakes.r: Mitigation reduces the CAUSES (emissions); adaptation copes with the EFFECTS, so sea walls are adaptation.
mistakes.w: Mixing up mitigation and adaptation, for example calling sea walls "mitigation".

mistakes.r: They reduce CO2 emissions by replacing fossil fuel electricity, which slows the enhanced greenhouse effect.
Trees absorb carbon dioxide in photosynthesis and store the carbon, which reduces the greenhouse effect.
mistakes.w: "Trees make oxygen so that cools the planet."

mistakes.r: CCS captures CO2, compresses it, transports it and stores it underground under cap rock; say how.
Explain: solar panels make electricity without burning fossil fuels, so less CO2 is emitted; also give a limitation.
mistakes.w: Naming strategies with no explanation, such as "use solar panels".

mistakes.r: Include drawbacks such as high initial cost, intermittent supply, visual impact or land use.
Kyoto set binding targets for developed countries only; Paris asks almost all countries to set their own targets.
Reservoirs increase supply; demand is reduced by metering, leak repair and water-saving devices.
Give a reasoned judgement, such as which strategy is most appropriate and why.
mistakes.w: Ending with no conclusion in 6 mark answers.

summary: The specification asks you to know how climate change is managed through mitigation (reducing causes: alternative energy, carbon capture, planting trees, international agreements) and adaptation (coping with effects: farming changes, water supply, rising sea level defences). It matters because it is the response part of the climate change topic and is regularly examined as 4 and 6 mark evaluation questions.

terms.d: A long-term change in global or regional climate patterns, now mainly linked to rising temperatures caused by human activity.
Strategies that reduce the causes of climate change by cutting greenhouse gas emissions or removing them from the atmosphere.
Strategies that help people and places cope with the effects of climate change, because some change is already unavoidable.
A gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that traps heat in the atmosphere and causes the enhanced greenhouse effect.
A natural or artificial store that absorbs more carbon than it releases, for example forests and oceans.
Energy sources such as wind, solar and hydro that do not run out and release little or no CO2 when generating electricity.
Coal, oil and natural gas formed from ancient organisms; burning them releases carbon dioxide.
Capturing CO2 from power stations and industry, transporting it and storing it underground in porous rock sealed by cap rock.
Planting trees in areas that have not recently been forest, to absorb CO2 by photosynthesis.
The removal of trees; it releases stored carbon and reduces the amount of CO2 absorbed.
A treaty between countries to set common targets, for example to reduce emissions (Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement).
Balancing the greenhouse gases emitted with an equal amount removed from the atmosphere.
A crop variety bred or modified to give reasonable yields with little water.
Removing salt from sea water to produce fresh water; it uses large amounts of energy.
Allowing the sea to flood low-value land and moving people and buildings inland instead of defending the coast.
Meeting present needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
When demand for water is greater than the amount available or when poor quality limits its use.

worked.q: A country's carbon dioxide emissions fell from 500 million tonnes to 380 million tonnes after it replaced coal power stations with wind farms. Calculate the percentage decrease. (2 marks)
steps: Percentage decrease = decrease / original x 100 = 120 / 500 x 100 = 24.

worked.ans: 43.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide avoided per day.
worked.q: A wind turbine produces on average 2 MW of electricity. A coal power station emits 0.9 tonnes of carbon dioxide for each megawatt-hour (MWh) of electricity it generates. Calculate the carbon dioxide avoided in one day if the turbine replaces coal electricity. (3 marks)
steps: Energy in one day = power x time = 2 MW x 24 h = 48 MWh.
CO2 avoided = 48 MWh x 0.9 tonnes per MWh = 43.2 tonnes.

worked.ans: Model answer: Mitigation tackles the causes by cutting emissions, for example wind farms replacing coal, so less carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere and the enhanced greenhouse effect weakens, though it is costly and slow to have an effect. Agreements like Paris spread responsibility, but targets are voluntary. Adaptation deals with effects, for example drought-resistant crops protect food supply and sea walls protect coastal homes, and the benefit is felt quickly, but it does not reduce the cause so costs keep rising. Overall a combination is most effective: mitigation is essential for the long term while adaptation protects people from changes already happening, and poorer countries often must prioritise adaptation.
worked.q: Assess the effectiveness of mitigation and adaptation strategies in managing climate change. (6 marks)
steps: Define: mitigation reduces the causes and adaptation copes with the effects.
Mitigation example with explanation: alternative energy such as wind replaces fossil fuels, so less CO2 is released and less heat is trapped; limitation is high set-up cost and intermittent supply.
International agreements such as the Paris Agreement share the effort globally, but targets are not always met.

Adaptation example: drought-resistant crops and efficient irrigation keep food production going when rainfall falls; sea walls protect coasts from rising seas but are expensive and do not stop warming.
Judgement: mitigation is vital long term because adaptation alone cannot stop the problem growing, but adaptation is needed now for changes already locked in.
